title: It was not a war. It was pest control that went badly.
description:
It was not a war. It was pest control that went badly. In November 1932 farmers in Western Australia's Wheatbelt asked for army machine guns against emus ruining their wheat. What followed looked far less organised than the name suggests.

Royal Australian Artillery. Commanded two Lewis guns and 10,000 rounds of ammunition against roughly 20,000 emus that had moved onto farmland, a target that would not hold still to be shot at.

Over 1,000 emus approached. The gun jammed after 12 were hit. Near a dam on 4 November, Meredith's men waited for the flock to come close before opening fire. One Lewis gun seized almost at once and the rest of the birds scattered.

Claimed by ordinary bounty hunters in just six months of 1934, under a scheme that had existed since 1923, far more than Meredith's whole campaign managed with soldiers and machine guns.

Paperwork did what the machine guns could not.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emu_War: read in full. Established the operational chronology (2 November 1932 first engagement, 4 November dam ambush where a Lewis gun jammed after 12 confirmed kills, 8 November withdrawal after 2,500 rounds fired, resumption on 13 November, recall on 10 December), Major G.P.W. Meredith's command of two Lewis guns and 10,000 rounds, his report claiming 986 confirmed kills from 9,860 rounds fired (a rate of exactly 10 rounds per kill, which historian Greg Beyer calls likely inflated), the roughly 20,000 emus that had moved onto Wheatbelt farmland, and the 1923 bounty scheme under which 57,034 bounties were claimed in six months of 1934, far exceeding the military operation's result.
